newsitem.title: USA: PLO assures U.S. of effort to halt terrorism.
newsitem.headline: PLO assures U.S. of effort to halt terrorism.

text.p: Palestinian negotiators assured the United States on Thursday that they were doing everything in their power to halt terrorism in a bid to get stalled peace talks with Israel back on track.

But the Palestinians continued to insist that Israel must stop all settlement activities on occupied Arab land as a condition for resuming negotiations, and U.S. officials held out no immediate hope of a breakthrough.

Negotiators Mahmoud Abbas and Saeb Erekat met Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and peace envoy Dennis Ross after Albright warned in a speech of an "unpredictable and dangerous" situation as a result of the deadlock.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said there was a lengthy discussion of security and that Albright "received strong assurances that the Palestinians will do all they can to stop terrorism".

"We want this effort ... to be serious and sustained, and I think it's fairly clear that the Palestinians are taking steps to thwart terrorism and that the security cooperation between the Israeli government and the Palestinian authorities has improved," Burns told reporters.
Erekat told journalists that Palestinians agreed "that peace and violence don't go together, and as Palestinians we do not condone or tolerate the killing of Israelis".

"On the contrary, we have been exerting more than 100 per cent efforts to stop the cycle of violence, counter-violence, and we will continue to do so, because we take this as a high priority for our national interest," he said.

Street battles have flared in the West Bank nearly every day since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on March 18, sent bulldozers to start work on a Jewish housing project on an East Jerusalem hill called Jabal Abu Ghneim by Arabs and Har Homa by Jews.

Israel has demanded that the Palestinians end the violence as a pre-condition for resuming peace talks, but Palestinians insist that Israel must stop work on the housing project, because Jerusalem is an issue to be negotiated.

Erekat said he had put to Albright "the ingredients that we think that can put the peace process back on track, and that is a cessation of all settlement activities, cessation of confiscation of land, including Jabal Abu Ghneim".
He also said any speed-up of so-called final status negotiations with Israel must go hand-in-hand with the implementation of existing pledges under the 1993 and 1995 Oslo peace accords.

It was not clear whether Erekat was signalling Palestinian acceptance of a proposal by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of fast-track talks on remaining issues that would end in six months rather than in 1999, as originally planned.
Burns said that following the talks with the Palestinians and, earlier in the week, with Netanyahu, the United States now needed to reflect on next steps.

"We have a certain confidence that we can work seriously to revive these talks. But I don't want to mislead you about any early dramatic progress ... I cannot say that we have moved far down the road toward the resumption of talks," he said.

Earlier, Albright said in a speech to the American Society of Newspaper Editors that "an unpredictable and dangerous situation" had been created by the "deterioration in the Arab-Israeli negotiating process".
"Arabs and Israelis alike have begun to lose faith in one another. The Oslo process and the working partnership between Israelis and Palestinians have broken down," she said.

In a concession to Israeli views she said there was "no moral equivalency between bulldozers and bombs," but she also said Israel should refrain from unilateral actions on issues that were to be negotiated -- a covert reference to Har Homa.
